top_comments.text:
I almost clicked away when you mentioned pork rinds—they are hard to find clean (without vegetable oils/maltodextrin) in the UK and prohibitively expensive at the butcher. I render pork skins myself when ordering online, but it’s a hassle when pressed for time.
Analysing the recipe: that is a lot of cheese! Delicious, but definitely more of an occasional treat than a daily carnivore staple.
As to the culinary method, here is why it fell short of your expectations:
Shrinkage & moisture loss: A large block of loose mince naturally contracts and expels liquid. Crimping the edges helps, but without an emulsified bind, it won’t hold.
Trapped steam: Layering 450 g of high-moisture cheese (especially cream cheese and mozzarella) between two raw meat layers in a deep Pyrex dish acts like a steam trap. Instead of distinct layers, it essentially boils the meat from the inside out while melting into a loose slurry.
Missing Maillard reaction: The trapped moisture and short 25-minute bake for a 1.6 kg mass leaves the beef dense, grey, and boiled rather than roasted and caramelised.
If you want this exact flavour profile without the structural collapse, Balkan cuisine solved this centuries ago with Uštipci and Punjena Pljeskavica:
Salt & Myosin (The Bind): Work the seasoned mince aggressively with salt (and traditionally a pinch of baking soda or sparkling water) until the proteins dissolve into a sticky, cohesive emulsion. This creates a tight net that locks in water and fat instead of squeezing out a greasewater puddle.
The Uštipci method: Dice the bacon and a hard cheese (like aged cheddar or semi-hard cheese) into small 5–8 mm cubes and knead them directly into the worked mince. Each cheese cube is individually insulated by its own envelope of meat, so the fat renders internally to flavour the meat while keeping each bite springy and juicy without leaking.
Portioning: Shape into 30–50 g balls or patties (silicone moulds work brilliantly in the air fryer). If you want a stuffed patty, roll two thin sheets of worked mince and seal the cheese inside with a wide crimped border—the protein bind welds shut on high heat.
I do feel curious to try and make your deep-dish version, it is such a time-saver; I guess, the best way to salvage it is to let it chill completely in the fridge and eat it cold as a meat terrine. Once the fat and cheese solidify, it slices cleanly; reheating a cut slice will simply leak all the cheese out again!

If i have to cook every meal, I won't do it.  It has to be easy.  So i do one big cooking session per week and make 25 meals or so, then the rest of the week, I eat from the freezer.
